hints: Think about what ions lithium and sulfur form by losing or gaining electrons to get a noble gas configuration.
walkthrough:
Work out the ion charges from the groups**
Lithium is in Group 1, so each Li atom loses one electron to form $\text{Li}^{+}$. Sulfur is in Group 16, so each S atom gains two electrons to form $\text{S}^{2-}$. In solid lithium sulfide the particles are these oppositely charged ions, in the ratio $2\text{Li}^{+}:1\text{S}^{2-}$ to give $\text{Li}_{2}\text{S}$.
Final answer: $\text{Li}^{+}$ and $\text{S}^{2-}$

hints: Picture the arrangement of ions in a crystalline ionic solid, a repeating 3D pattern rather than separate molecules.
Consider what type and strength of attraction holds oppositely charged ions together and what energy is needed to break it on melting.
walkthrough:
See the structure as giant, not molecular**
In the crystal there are no $\text{Li}_{2}\text{S}$ molecules. Instead $\text{Li}^{+}$ and $\text{S}^{2-}$ ions pack together in a regular repeating 3D arrangement called a giant ionic lattice. Every ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.

Link strong attractions to high melting point**
Between the ions there are strong electrostatic attractions, the ionic bonds, acting in all directions throughout the lattice. Melting means loosening this rigid lattice so ions can move. Because so many strong attractions must be broken, a very large amount of thermal energy is needed, giving the high melting point of $938^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: Lithium sulfide has a giant ionic lattice.
There are many strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions, requiring a large amount of thermal energy to break, so melting point is high.

hints: Compare with a normal shared pair where each atom supplies one electron, then think what is different about who supplies the electrons here.
walkthrough:
Focus on the origin of the shared pair**
A normal covalent bond is one shared pair with one electron from each atom. A coordinate bond, also called a dative covalent bond, is still a shared pair of electrons, but both electrons come from the same atom. Once formed it is identical in strength to any other covalent bond.
Final answer: A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair are provided by the same atom / species.

hints: Count outer electrons first, C brings 4 (x) and O brings 6 (dot), for 10 electrons total to place around C and O.
Remember CO has a triple bond with one lone pair left on each atom, and think which atom must supply both electrons for one of those three bonds.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons to place**
C is Group 14 so show 4 x. O is Group 16 so show 6 $\bullet$. That is 10 outer electrons in total. You need to arrange them to give each atom a stable octet.

Build the triple bond with a coordinate bond**
Place three bonding pairs between C and O. Two of these are normal covalent bonds, one x with one $\bullet$ each. The third is the coordinate bond, with both electrons from O, so two $\bullet$ shared with C. That gives 2 x and 4 $\bullet$ in the bonding region.

Add the two lone pairs**
C has used 2 of its 4 x in bonding, so the remaining 2 x sit on C as a lone pair. O has used 4 of its 6 $\bullet$ in bonding, so the remaining 2 $\bullet$ sit on O as a lone pair. Check: C is surrounded by 8 electrons, O is surrounded by 8 electrons.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram showing C triple bonded to O:
Three shared pairs between C and O containing 2 x and 4 $\bullet$.
One lone pair on C of 2 x and one lone pair on O of 2 $\bullet$. Total 4 x around C and 6 $\bullet$ around O.

hints: Think about the two simplifications an ideal gas makes, one about the size of the particles compared to the container and one about attractions between them.
Recall what is assumed about energy loss when particles collide with each other and the walls.
walkthrough:
Picture a perfect, simplified gas**
An ideal gas imagines molecules as tiny point particles flying around an almost empty container. So assumption 1: the volume of the molecules themselves is negligible compared to the total volume of the gas.

Remove attractions and energy loss**
Assumption 2: there are no forces of attraction or repulsion between molecules. They move randomly and independently. In addition, all collisions with each other and the walls are elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost.

Final answer: Any two from:
Particles have negligible volume / size compared to volume of container.
No intermolecular forces / interactions between particles.
Collisions are elastic.

hints: Think what high pressure does to the distance between $\text{N}_{2}$ molecules and why attractions can no longer be ignored.
Think what happens to the space taken up by the molecules themselves when the gas is highly compressed.
walkthrough:
See why closeness brings attractions into play**
At normal pressure $\text{N}_{2}$ molecules are far apart, so attractions are negligible. At very high pressure they are squeezed very close together, so London dispersion forces between them become significant. The no forces assumption breaks down.

See why molecular size now matters**
Squeezing also means the empty space is much smaller, so the actual volume occupied by the $\text{N}_{2}$ molecules themselves is a significant fraction of the container volume. It can no longer be treated as zero, so $\text{N}_{2}$ deviates from ideal behaviour.

Final answer: At very high pressure molecules are very close together so intermolecular forces become significant.
The volume of the molecules is no longer negligible compared to the total volume.

hints: Start with the force present in all molecular substances, even non-polar $\text{N}_{2}$, and check the electron numbers to compare its strength.
Use the tick and cross for dipole moment to decide which gas has an extra permanent dipole force in addition, explaining its higher boiling point.
walkthrough:
Give both gases the universal force**
Every simple molecular substance has London dispersion forces, correctly called instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces. Both $\text{N}_{2}$ and CO have 14 electrons per molecule, so this contribution is very similar in strength for both.

Add the extra force for the polar molecule**
The table shows $\text{N}_{2}$ has no dipole moment, it is non-polar, so it has only instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces. CO has a dipole moment, it is polar, so it has permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces in addition. These extra attractions need more energy to break, which fits the slightly higher boiling point of CO ($-191.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ versus $-195.8^{\circ}\text{C}$).

Final answer: $\text{N}_{2}(\text{g})$: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces only.
$\text{CO}(\text{g})$: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces and permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.

hints: Think about which atom in C-O pulls the shared bonding electrons more strongly toward itself.
walkthrough:
Link unequal sharing to electronegativity**
Oxygen attracts a shared pair of electrons more strongly than carbon does. Because O is more electronegative than C, the bonding electrons sit closer to O, giving O a partial negative charge and C a partial positive charge. That charge separation is the dipole moment.
Final answer: O is more electronegative than C, so bonding electrons are pulled towards O creating a dipole.
